messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Hans Becker is a 76-year-old widowed man who came for treatment after months of insisting to himself that he ought to be able to manage on his own. He works part-time as a cashier in a neighborhood grocery store, a routine he took up after his wife died because he wanted structure and some contact with people. He had spent part of his youth as a civilian in a war zone in Europe, and although he had carried those memories quietly for decades, they returned with force in later life. What stays with him are not long coherent stories but stark visual fragments: a street blown open, shattered glass glittering in the air, the fixed look on a stranger’s face, the inside of a vehicle he had been trying to reach as shelling began nearby. At times he can describe these scenes in a flat, distant way, almost as if they happened to someone else. At other times an image seizes him so completely that he feels he is there again in the danger, not remembering but reliving.

Over the years Hans had come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that whatever trust he once had in other people, life, and God had worn away in that period. As these beliefs hardened, the old memories seemed to return with even more force. When he thought, as he often did, about why this had happened to him and what it had meant, he never arrived at comfort; instead he found himself staring again at those frozen pictures, convinced they proved what he already feared about the world. The memories in turn deepened the same conclusions. When a vivid image broke through, he was left certain afterward that nowhere is really safe and that something essential in him had been permanently damaged.

He speaks painfully about no longer being capable of the things that once defined him. Driving is the clearest example. He used to take pride in handling himself, in going where he pleased without relying on anyone. Now even riding in a car feels intolerable. The images tied to vehicles and sudden attack are so immediate that he avoids driving altogether and refuses lifts unless there is no other option. He has begun arranging his life around buses, short walks, and rides from a neighbor only when absolutely necessary. That restriction has made him feel older and diminished, and each new workaround seems to confirm his belief that he is not the man he used to be.

At the grocery store, these problems are woven into ordinary moments. Standing at his register, Hans watches customers closely, scanning faces, hands, tone of voice, any sign that someone might turn aggressive. If a man comes in tense or loud, Hans feels his body brace before he has consciously thought anything. He keeps himself on guard all day and has trouble settling even at night, lying awake because some part of him feels he must remain alert. When his guard is this high, the war memories come more easily; a customer’s expression, the slam of a cart, or the glimpse of a car through the front windows can pull up a visual flash so sharply that for a second he is not in the store but back in danger. And the more he lives in this state of watchfulness, the more convinced he becomes that his vigilance is justified, that people cannot be trusted and that the world will hurt you if you stop looking.

In response, Hans has narrowed his life further. He avoids cars, but he also pushes away positive feelings when they arise, because relief or pleasure feels unsafe, like letting his guard down. On better days he distrusts the lightness almost immediately. He also spends long stretches turning the trauma over in his mind, trying to understand why it happened and why it has followed him into old age. None of this brings peace. Pushing away good moments leaves him more fixed on danger, and all the searching for meaning seems only to circle him back to the same images and the same bleak conclusions. The less room he allows himself for ordinary ease, the more jumpy he becomes; the more he stays on edge, the more he feels the world has proven him right.

By the time he sought help, Hans was exhausted. Sleep had become fragmented by the felt need to stay alert, work was harder because he could not stop monitoring customers, and his dependence on others for transportation humiliated him. What finally brought him in was the fear that his life was shrinking to the size of his precautions. He said he was afraid that if this continued, he would spend whatever years he had left trapped between old pictures and constant watchfulness. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not happiness exactly, but the possibility of feeling safe enough to rest and to believe that he is still capable of living as himself.
